slides.title: Certificates
points: Digital certificates bind identities to public keys and rely on certificate authorities, trust chains, and status mechanisms.
Security+ Objective 1.4: explain the importance of using appropriate cryptographic solutions.

slides.title: Certificate Authority (CA)
slides.teach: A trusted entity that issues and digitally signs certificates.

course.learn: A trusted entity that issues and digitally signs certificates.

breakdown.explanation: The CA vouches for the binding between an identity and a public key.

course.why: Clients can trust certificates that chain to trusted certificate authorities.
course.example: A browser trusts a website certificate because it chains to a recognized CA.

slides.title: Certificate Revocation List (CRL)
slides.teach: A published list of certificates revoked before normal expiration.

course.learn: A published list of certificates revoked before normal expiration.

breakdown.explanation: Download or check a list of revoked certificates.

course.why: A certificate may need to stop being trusted before its expiration date.
course.example: A compromised certificate is added to the CA's revocation list.
course.check_q: Which method uses a published list of revoked certificates?

slides.title: Online Certificate Status Protocol (OCSP)
slides.teach: An online protocol used to check the revocation status of a specific certificate.

course.learn: An online protocol used to check the revocation status of a specific certificate.

breakdown.explanation: Ask an online responder about one certificate.

course.why: It can provide more targeted certificate-status checking than downloading a full list.
course.example: A browser queries an OCSP responder for the status of one site certificate.
course.check_q: Which protocol checks one certificate's status online?

slides.title: Self-signed Certificate
slides.teach: A certificate signed by its own key rather than by an external trusted CA.

course.learn: A certificate signed by its own key rather than by an external trusted CA.
course.why: It can be useful internally but is not automatically trusted by normal external clients.
course.example: A test server uses a self-signed certificate and browsers show a trust warning.
course.check_q: Which certificate is signed by itself?

slides.title: Third-party Certificate
slides.teach: A certificate issued and signed by a trusted external or organizational CA.

course.learn: A certificate issued and signed by a trusted external or organizational CA.

breakdown.explanation: A trusted CA vouches for the certificate.

course.why: It can chain to a trusted root recognized by clients.
course.example: A public website uses a certificate issued by a recognized CA.
course.check_q: Which certificate is issued by a trusted CA?

slides.title: Root of Trust
slides.teach: A highly trusted starting point from which additional trust relationships are derived.

course.learn: A highly trusted starting point from which additional trust relationships are derived.

breakdown.explanation: Trust begins at a trusted root and can extend through a chain.

course.why: Certificate validation depends on a chain terminating at a root the client already trusts.
course.example: A browser validates a site certificate through an intermediate CA to a trusted root CA.
course.exam: Root of trust = TRUST STARTS HERE.
course.check_q: What is the trusted starting point of a certificate chain?

slides.title: Certificate Signing Request (CSR)
slides.teach: A request sent to a CA containing identifying information and a public key so a certificate can be issued.

course.learn: A request sent to a CA containing identifying information and a public key so a certificate can be issued.

breakdown.explanation: Send identity + public key; keep the private key private.

course.why: The CA needs the public key and identity information to create a certificate.
course.example: A server generates a key pair and sends a CSR to a CA while retaining the private key.
course.exam: CSR = PUBLIC KEY GOES OUT; PRIVATE KEY STAYS.
course.check_q: Which key should be included in a CSR?

slides.title: Wildcard Certificate
slides.teach: A certificate that can cover multiple subdomains matching a domain pattern.

course.learn: A certificate that can cover multiple subdomains matching a domain pattern.

breakdown.explanation: One certificate can cover many matching subdomains.

course.why: It can simplify certificate deployment across multiple subdomains.
course.example: One certificate protects mail.example.com and portal.example.com.
course.check_q: What certificate can cover multiple matching subdomains?

blocks.title: Who issued it, is it revoked, and what key leaves the server?
items: A CA signs certificates to vouch for the binding between identity and public key.
Example: A browser trusts a site because its certificate chains to a trusted CA.
The client checks a published list of revoked certificates.
Example: A compromised certificate appears on the CA's CRL.
The client asks for the current status of a specific certificate.
Example: A browser queries an OCSP responder.
The certificate signs itself, so clients need an explicit trust decision.
Example: A test server uses a self-signed certificate.
CSR → PUBLIC KEY OUT, PRIVATE KEY STAYS
The CSR contains the public key and identity information; the private key remains with the requester.
Example: A web server generates a key pair and sends a CSR to a CA.
One wildcard certificate can cover multiple hosts matching the wildcard pattern.
Example: *.example.com can cover mail.example.com and portal.example.com.
blocks.example: Memory: CA issues · CRL list · OCSP online · CSR public key · Wildcard subdomains.

questions.q: Which trusted entity issues and digitally signs certificates?
questions.explanation: A certificate authority issues and signs certificates.

questions.q: A client downloads a published list of certificates that should no longer be trusted. Which mechanism is this?
questions.explanation: A CRL is a published list of revoked certificates.

questions.q: A browser asks an online responder for the revocation status of one certificate. Which protocol is being used?
questions.explanation: OCSP provides online status checking for a specific certificate.

questions.q: A lab server uses a certificate signed by its own key, causing normal browsers to show a trust warning. What type of certificate is this?
questions.explanation: A self-signed certificate is signed by itself and is not automatically externally trusted.

questions.q: A public website wants a certificate that chains to a CA already trusted by browsers. Which type is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: A third-party certificate issued by a trusted CA can chain to a recognized root.

questions.q: What is the highly trusted starting point from which a certificate chain derives trust?
questions.explanation: A trusted root is the starting point for certificate-chain trust.

questions.q: A server generates a key pair and sends a request to a CA to obtain a certificate. What should the request include?
choices: The public key and identifying information
questions.explanation: A CSR includes the public key and identifying information; the private key should remain with the requester.

questions.q: Which certificate can cover multiple matching subdomains such as mail.example.com and portal.example.com?
questions.explanation: A wildcard certificate can cover multiple subdomains that match the wildcard pattern.

questions.q: A certificate's private key is compromised before the certificate expires. Which mechanism can publish that the certificate should no longer be trusted?
questions.explanation: A CRL can list certificates revoked before expiration.

questions.q: Which statement about a CSR is correct?
choices: The public key is included, while the private key should remain with the requester
The private key is sent to the CA
A CSR is a revocation list
A CSR is an online status protocol
questions.explanation: The requester retains the private key and sends the public key in the CSR.
